questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation Given a Corresponding Perfect Square
questions.problem:
Solve the equation $-6{y}^{2}+24y=21.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${y}^{2}-4y+4$ is a perfect square.*
questions.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{y}^{2}-4y+4=(y-2)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{y}^{2}+24y & =21 \\ -6({y}^{2}-4y) & =21 \\ -6({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y) & =21 \\ -6({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}) & =21 \\ -6[(y-2)^{2}-{2}^{2}] & =21 \\ -6[(y-2)^{2}-4] & =21 \\ -6(y-2)^{2}+(-6)(-4) & =21 \\ -6(y-2)^{2}+24 & =21\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $24$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-6),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6(y-2)^{2}+24 & =21 \\ -6(y-2)^{2}+24-24 & =21-24 \\ -6(y-2)^{2} & =-3 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =\frac{(-3)}{(-6)} \\ (y-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{(y-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ |y-2| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ y-2 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ y & =2\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the equation $5{y}^{2}-40y=-76.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${y}^{2}-8y+16$ is a perfect square.*
questions.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{y}^{2}-8y+16=(y-4)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2}-40y & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-8y) & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-2\cdot 4y) & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-2\cdot 4y+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2}) & =-76 \\ 5[(y-4)^{2}-{4}^{2}] & =-76 \\ 5[(y-4)^{2}-16] & =-76 \\ 5(y-4)^{2}-80 & =-76\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $80$ to both sides and then dividing by $5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5(y-4)^{2}-80 & =-76 \\ 5(y-4)^{2}-80+80 & =-76+80 \\ 5(y-4)^{2} & =4 \\ (y-4)^{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-4)^{2} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ \sqrt{(y-4)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{5}} \\ |y-4| & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ y-4 & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ y & =4\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the equation $-4{x}^{2}+4x=-2.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}$ is a perfect square.*
questions.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}={(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}+4x & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-x) & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x) & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =-2 \\ -4[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =-2 \\ -4[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-4)(-\frac{1}{4}) & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1 & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $1$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-4),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1 & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1-1 & =-2-1 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =-3 \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{(-3)}{(-4)} \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\ |x-\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x-\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the equation $4{x}^{2}+24x=-11.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}+6x+9$ is a perfect square.*
questions.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+24x & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+6x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-{3}^{2}] & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-9] & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $36$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36+36 & =-11+36 \\ 4(x+3)^{2} & =25 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |x+3| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ x+3 & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-3\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{11}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}^{2}+6y+9=(y+3)^{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-7{y}^{2}-42y & =62 \\ -7({y}^{2}+6y) & =62 \\ -7({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y) & =62 \\ -7({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) & =62 \\ -7[(y+3)^{2}-{3}^{2}] & =62 \\ -7[(y+3)^{2}-9] & =62 \\ -7(y+3)^{2}+(-7)(-9) & =62 \\ -7(y+3)^{2}+63 & =62\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $63$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-7),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-7(y+3)^{2}+63 & =62 \\ -7(y+3)^{2}+63-63 & =62-63 \\ -7(y+3)^{2} & =-1 \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{(-1)}{(-7)} \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{1}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem: The equation $6{z}^{2}+10z-1=0$ can be written in the form $6(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}6{z}^{2}+10z-1 & =0 \\ 6{z}^{2}+10z & =1 \\ 6({z}^{2}+\frac{5}{3}z) & =1 \\ 6[{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{6}\cdot z+{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 6[{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 6[{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-\frac{25}{36}] & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{25}{36} & =1 \\ 6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-\frac{25}{6} & =1 \\ 6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2} & =\frac{31}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{5}{6}$ and $q=\frac{31}{6}.$ Finally,

$$
p+q=\frac{5}{6}+\frac{31}{6}=\frac{36}{6}=6.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-5 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =5 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{29}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}$ and $q=\frac{29}{4}.$ Finally,

$$
p+q=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{29}{4}=\frac{32}{4}=8.

questions.problem: The equation $3{x}^{2}-4x+1=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-4x+1 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4x & =-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4x & =-1 \\ 3({x}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}x) & =-1 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{2}{3}x+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}] & =-1 \\ 3[{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-\frac{4}{9}] & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-3\cdot \frac{4}{9} & =-1 \\ 3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-\frac{4}{3} & =-1 \\ 3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2} & =-1+\frac{4}{3} \\ 3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{2}{3}$ and $q=\frac{1}{3}.$

First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-4x-9 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-4x & =9 \\ 2({x}^{2}-2x) & =9 \\ 2[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{(1)}^{2}-{(1)}^{2}] & =9 \\ 2[{(x-1)}^{2}-1] & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-1)}^{2}-2\cdot 1 & =9 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2}-2 & =9 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2} & =9+2 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2} & =11\end{aligned}
$$

So, $q=11.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-1)}^{2} & =11 \\ {(x-1)}^{2} & =\frac{11}{2} \\ \sqrt{{(x-1)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ |x-1| & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The equation $-3{x}^{2}-2x+6=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}-2x+6) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+2x-6 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x & =6 \\ 3[{x}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x] & =6 \\ 3[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}x+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}] & =6 \\ 3[{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{9}] & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-3\cdot \frac{1}{9} & =6 \\ 3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{3} & =6 \\ 3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2} & =6+\frac{1}{3} \\ 3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2} & =\frac{19}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{1}{3}$, $q=\frac{19}{3}.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=\frac{19}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{18}{3}=6.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Solve the equation $-2x^2 - 4x = 1.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that $x^2 + 2x + 1$ is a perfect square.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
x^2 + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)^2.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}-4x & =1 \\ -2({x}^{2}+2x) & =1 \\ -2({x}^{2}+2\cdot 1x) & =1 \\ -2({x}^{2}+2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =1 \\ -2[(x+1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =1 \\ -2[(x+1)^{2}-1] & =1 \\ -2(x+1)^{2}+(-2)(-1) & =1 \\ -2(x+1)^{2}+2 & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $2$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-2),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2(x+1)^{2}+2 & =1 \\ -2(x+1)^{2}+2-2 & =1-2 \\ -2(x+1)^{2} & =-1 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{(-1)}{(-2)} \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{(x+1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ |x+1| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ x+1 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ x & =-1\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Positive Leading Coefficient
canonical_examples.problem: Write the equation $2x^2 - 6x = 1$ in the form $(x+p)^2 = q,$ and hence solve the equation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we divide out by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-6x & =1 \\ 2({x}^{2}-3x) & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-3x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot (\frac{3}{2})\cdot x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =\frac{2}{4} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{11}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-\dfrac32$ and $q=\dfrac{11}{4}.$ Now, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{4}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{2} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{3\pm \sqrt{11}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
canonical_examples.problem: Write the equation $-2x^2+2x+1 = 0$ in the form $2(x+p)^2=q,$ and hence solve the equation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-2{x}^{2}+2x+1) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2x-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-2x-1 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2x & =1 \\ 2({x}^{2}-x) & =1 \\ 2[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 2[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =1 \\ 2{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ 2{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\dfrac12$ and $q=\dfrac32.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\ |x-\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x-\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
